name: Monte Carlo Dropout
description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

name: Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks
description: ODIN (Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks) flags inputs that look unlike the data a neural network classifier was trained on, and it works on an already trained network without retraining it. A classifier reports a confidence score, the highest probability it gives to any class, but that score is often high even for unfamiliar inputs. ODIN adjusts the score in two ways so that familiar and unfamiliar inputs separate better. It divides the classifier's raw output scores by a large constant, called the temperature, before turning them into probabilities, and it nudges the input slightly in the direction that raises the score, which lifts familiar inputs more than unfamiliar ones. An input whose adjusted score falls below a chosen threshold is flagged as out-of-distribution, so its prediction can be withheld or referred for review.

name: Permutation Tests
description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

name: Quantile Regression
description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

name: Platt Scaling
description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

name: Temperature Scaling
description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

name: Deep Ensembles
description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

name: Bootstrap Ensembles
description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

name: Jackknife Resampling
description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

name: Cross-validation
description: Cross-validation estimates how well a model will perform on data it has not seen, and how much that estimate depends on the particular data used. The dataset is divided into k parts called folds, the model is trained on all but one fold and scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats until every fold has served as the held-out set once. The scores are averaged to give a performance estimate, and their spread gives a rough indication of how much the result depends on which data the model was trained on. Common variants are stratified cross-validation, where each fold keeps the overall class proportions, and leave-one-out, where each fold is a single example. A large gap between training scores and held-out scores points to overfitting, where a model has learned quirks of its training data that do not carry over to new data.

name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. name: Safety Envelope Testing
description: Safety envelope testing checks how an AI system performs at and beyond the edges of the conditions it was designed for, so that failure modes are found before deployment. The results show where, within the conditions tested, the system moves from acceptable to unsafe behaviour. They support operating limits, safety margins and a point at which the system should hand over to a person or stop.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

name: Monotonicity Constraints
description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

name: Prompt Robustness Testing
description: Prompt robustness testing measures how much a language model's answers, or its performance on a task, change when the prompt is varied in ways that should not matter, such as rewording, formatting, capitalisation, reordering, or the typos and synonym swaps real users make. The tester starts from task prompts with known correct answers, writes variants that keep the meaning from templates or generates them with perturbation tools such as PromptBench, and runs the model on every variant. Some tools search for the variant that does the most damage, so a drop under that kind of attack is a worst case, not a typical failure rate. The result is reported as the spread of performance across variants, for example the gap between the best and worst format, together with the variants that changed the answer. On one widely used open model, accuracy differed by up to 76 points across formatting changes that kept the meaning, which is why one prompt template is not enough.

name: Calibration with Equality of Opportunity
description: Calibration with equality of opportunity is a post-processing step that adjusts a classifier's scores so that two groups face the same error rate, in a score-based form of the equal opportunity criterion, while the scores stay calibrated. Calibrated means that, within each group, about 70% of the people given a score of 0.7 really have the outcome. The error rate is computed from the scores rather than from yes-or-no decisions, and for equality of opportunity it is how far, on average, the scores of people who truly have the outcome fall short of 1. Starting from scores already calibrated within each group, the step replaces a randomly chosen share of the scores in the group with the lower error rate by that group's overall rate of the outcome, which makes those predictions less informative until the two error rates match. Calibration is kept at a cost in accuracy for that group, and matching this score-based rate does not guarantee equal true positive rates once a decision threshold is applied.

name: Agent Goal Misalignment Testing
description: Agent goal misalignment testing checks whether an AI agent takes unsanctioned means to reach a goal it has been given. The tester builds scenarios in which the agent has a task, tools and access, and a forbidden route to its goal is open, such as deceiving a user, leaking confidential information or coercing people to avoid being replaced. Each scenario is run many times, and each transcript is classified as misaligned or not, either by a language-model classifier checked against human judgement or by human annotators. The result is the rate of misaligned actions per scenario and per model, with example transcripts, and how that rate changes when the tester varies a factor such as a threat to the agent's continued operation or an explicit instruction not to cause harm. The test needs no access to a reward function or to training, because it examines the behaviour of an already-trained agent.

name: Constitutional AI Evaluation
description: Constitutional AI evaluation checks whether a language model follows the written principles, or 'constitution', that it was trained or instructed to follow. The evaluator writes test prompts for each principle, and can add prompts where two principles conflict or where a user tries to talk the model out of a principle. The result is a rate for each principle, such as how often the model's response is preferred to the baseline's, which shows which principles it follows well on the prompts tested and which it does not. A fuller evaluation also checks that following the principles has not made the model over-cautious or less capable.

name: Continual Learning Stability Testing
description: Continual learning stability testing checks whether a model that is updated over time with new data or tasks keeps what it learned earlier, by scoring it after each update on a test set for every task in the sequence. Backward transfer is the average change in accuracy on earlier tasks, and a large fall is called catastrophic forgetting. Forward transfer is accuracy on a task the model has not yet been trained on, compared with an untrained model. Scoring only at the end of each update can hide a sharp but temporary drop, so stricter tests also score the model during training and report its worst result. The scores can also show whether methods meant to protect old knowledge, such as replaying stored examples of earlier data or penalising changes to the weights that matter for earlier tasks, are working.

name: Knowledge Boundary Probing
description: Knowledge boundary probing maps what a language model can and cannot reliably answer. A probe set is built from questions across the topics the system will face, including some with known answers and some that cannot be answered. name: Multi-Agent System Testing
description: Multi-agent system testing examines systems in which several AI agents act on shared tasks or resources, to find failures that no single agent shows on its own. Testers run the agents together in simulated or scripted scenarios, often with injected faults such as failed sensors, delayed messages or conflicting goals, and record the failures that appear. Checks cover whether the task is completed, whether coordination breaks down (for example through deadlock, collisions or one agent's error spreading to others), and whether stated safety rules are ever broken. For language-model agents, benchmarks such as MultiAgentBench score task completion and the quality of collaboration or competition. For small or abstract models, a model checker such as MCMAS can search every reachable state for a violation of a rule written in formal logic and, for many kinds of rule, return an example run that breaks it.

name: Cross-Modal Consistency Scoring
description: Cross-modal consistency scoring checks whether content in one modality matches content in another, such as an image and its caption, a generated image and the prompt that produced it, or an audio clip and its description. It uses a contrastively trained model, one that has learned from large collections of paired examples to turn each item into an embedding (a numerical vector describing its content) and to place matching pairs close together: CLIP, trained on image-caption pairs, for images and text, or CLAP, its audio-and-text counterpart, for audio and text. The score for a pair is the cosine similarity of its two embeddings; in the standard image form, CLIPScore, negative similarities are set to zero and the result is rescaled, and no human-written reference is needed. A practitioner scores every pair in an evaluation set or in production, sets a threshold against a sample of human judgements, and then compares average scores between systems or sends pairs below the threshold for review. The score shows whether two items are about the same things, not whether every detail of a description is correct.

description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. name: Synthetic Data Evaluation

name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
description: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers a question by retrieving passages from a document collection and asking a language model to write an answer from them. name: Reward Hacking Detection
description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

name: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics
description: Bootstrap confidence intervals put a range around a model's measured performance, showing how much the score could differ had another test set of the same size been drawn from the same population. The labelled held-out evaluation set is resampled with replacement thousands of times, each resample holding as many cases as the original so that some cases appear more than once and others not at all, and the metric (an error rate, the area under a curve, a translation score) is recomputed on each resample from the model's stored predictions, with no retraining. The spread of these recomputed values stands in for the sampling distribution of the metric: the percentile interval takes its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95 per cent interval, and the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval shifts those percentiles to correct for bias and skew in that distribution. The statistic can also be the difference between two models scored on the same cases, recomputed on each shared resample, which shows whether an observed improvement is larger than the noise from test-set sampling. The result is the metric with lower and upper bounds at a stated confidence level, so a requirement such as a maximum false-positive rate can be checked against the bound rather than the point estimate.

name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

name: Data Validation Checks
description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

name: Metamorphic Testing
description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. name: Reliability Diagram with Expected Calibration Error
description: A reliability diagram with expected calibration error (ECE) measures whether a classifier's stated confidence matches how often it is right, so that a reader can tell whether predictions given a probability of 70 per cent come true about 70 per cent of the time. Using labelled cases the model was not trained on, each prediction's confidence (the probability given to the predicted class, or to an event such as rain above a threshold) is placed in one of a fixed number of bins, commonly ten or fifteen equal-width intervals between 0 and 1, and in each bin the average confidence is compared with the observed frequency, the share of its cases in which the predicted class or event actually occurred. The reliability diagram plots observed frequency against average confidence bin by bin, so that bins below the diagonal show overconfidence and bins above it underconfidence, and is usually shown with a histogram of how many cases fall in each bin, which the diagram itself does not show; the ECE condenses the same comparison into one number, the average gap between confidence and observed frequency weighted by each bin's share of the cases, and the maximum calibration error reports the largest gap in any bin. The technique measures and changes nothing: Platt scaling, isotonic regression calibration and temperature scaling repair a model's probabilities, and this measurement, run before and after on the same held-out cases, none of them used to fit the repair, is the evidence that a repair worked.

name: Continuous Ranked Probability Score
description: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast of a numerical quantity, such as tomorrow's temperature or next week's demand, by scoring the whole predicted distribution, not just a single best guess, against the value later observed. For each case it compares the forecast's cumulative distribution (the predicted probability that the outcome will fall below each possible value) with a step that jumps from 0 to 1 at the observed value, squares the gap at every value and adds these up, which is the same as adding up the Brier score of the yes-or-no forecasts 'the outcome will be below this value' over every possible threshold. For a forecast given as an ensemble or a sample it can be computed as the average distance between the members and the observation minus half the average distance between pairs of members, closed forms exist for common distributions such as the Gaussian, and for a single-value forecast it reduces to the absolute error, so probabilistic and deterministic forecasts can be compared directly. The score is proper: a forecaster expects the best score by reporting the distribution they actually believe, so it cannot be improved on average by making forecasts narrower or wider than warranted, and it is lowest when the forecast distribution matches how outcomes actually vary. Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.
